summary: Explains for novice users what FTP is, what anonymous FTP is, and what an anonymous FTP archive site is. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A beginner's guide to a public file-sharing library you can visit without an account.

how do you use anonymous ftp
subtitle: A beginner's guide to finding and downloading files from public Internet archives.

tldr.problem: Novice Internet users did not understand how to access the wealth of software, documents, and data available at archive sites, or how to unpack compressed and bundled files once downloaded.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1635 explains the FTP protocol, the anonymous account mechanism used by archive sites, the file naming conventions for compressed formats (tar, gzip, zip), and walks through a sample session step by step.
tldr.outcome: This memo became an essential reference for users learning to navigate the early Internet's file archives, establishing conventions and best practices still used in open-source software distribution today.

facts.label: Compression formats documented
facts.value: 13 (tar, compress, gzip, zip, uuencode, binhex, zoo, shar, and others)

today: RFC 1635 is an Informational RFC (FYI 24) from 1994 documenting the then-dominant file transfer mechanism on the Internet. While FTP remains available, it is now used primarily for specific applications and organizations; the World Wide Web and HTTP replaced FTP for most public file distribution. Modern software distribution uses tools like Git and package managers rather than FTP archives.

sections.title: What is FTP and Anonymous FTP?
sections.content:
FTP (File Transfer Protocol) is one of the oldest protocols in the TCP/IP suite, dating to the early days of the Internet. FTP makes it possible to transfer files from one computer (host) to another. Normally, users with accounts on both systems could log in with a username and password to transfer their own files. However, archive sites created a special mechanism called anonymous FTP to allow general public access.

An anonymous account is a special username ('anonymous') on archive sites with limited permissions: users can log in (using 'guest' or their email address as a password), browse a limited set of directories, and download (retrieve) files. Crucially, anonymous users cannot upload files to the archive. Traditionally, archive operators created this account as a courtesy to share their information with the broader Internet community. Archive sites became repositories of software, documents, standards, and data—essentially libraries where anyone could browse and borrow without needing a personal account.
sections.eli5: FTP is the old-fashioned way to download files from the Internet. Most archive sites let anyone log in as 'anonymous' and grab what they want. You just need to know the computer's address and the file's location.

sections.title: Connecting and Downloading
sections.content:
To start an FTP session, a user types ftp followed by either the fully-qualified domain name (e.g., naic.nasa.gov) or the IP address (e.g., 128.102.128.6) of the archive host. The server responds with a banner and prompts for a username. The user types anonymous; the server then asks for a password. By convention, the user provides either guest or their email address (a courtesy that helps operators understand who is using the service).

Once logged in, the user navigates using familiar commands: cd to change directories, ls or dir to list files, and get filename to retrieve a file. Important files to look for are README, 00README.1ST, INDEX, or similar—these explain what is in the directory. The user can also retrieve multiple files at once using mget with a wildcard pattern. File transfer mode matters: ascii for text files (the default), binary for executable programs and data files that use all 8 bits per byte. When finished, the user types quit to close the connection.
sections.eli5: You type 'ftp' and a server name, log in as 'anonymous', and then use commands like 'cd' and 'get' to find and download files. It is like navigating folders on a computer, but over the network.

sections.title: Compression and Bundling Formats
sections.content:
Internet archives used file naming conventions to help users understand how files were transformed for storage and transport. Compression reduced file size to save disk space and bandwidth: .Z files used UNIX compress, .gz or .z files used GNU gzip, .zip and .arc were common on PCs. Bundling grouped multiple files into one: .tar (tape archive) was the UNIX standard. Transformation converted binary files to printable ASCII for email transport: .uu files were uuencoded, .atob was ASCII-to-binary, .hqx (binhex) was for Macintosh.

Files often combined multiple processes, producing names like patch.tar.Z (bundled with tar, then compressed). The RFC documents over a dozen formats including compress/uncompress, atob/btoa, uuencode/uudecode, tar/untar, zip/unzip, arc/unarc, binhex, shar, zoo, and gzip. It also explains that some operating systems replaced multiple periods with hyphens or underscores due to filename length limits. A practical example: to unpack patch.tar.Z, the user would type uncompress patch.tar.Z (creating patch.tar), then tar xvf patch.tar (extracting individual files with verbose output).
sections.eli5: Files at archives have special suffixes showing how they were squished or bundled. .tar means files are glued together. .Z or .gz means squished. The RFC explains 13 different ways archives package files and how to unpack each one.

sections.title: Sample FTP Session
sections.content:
The RFC provides a detailed walkthrough of an actual FTP session connecting to naic.nasa.gov (NASA Network Applications and Information Center). The user executes ftp naic.nasa.gov, receives a welcome banner, logs in as anonymous (providing an email address as password), and sees additional information about accessing NAIC via Gopher and World-Wide-Web (showing this was written during the transition from FTP dominance to the web). The user then cd files/rfc to navigate to the RFC directory, sees a README.rfc file listed, and retrieves RFC 959 (the FTP specification) using get rfc959.txt.

Key observations from the example: every server response is preceded by a reply code (220, 331, 230, 250, 200, 150, 226, 221) defined in RFC 959. The password is not echoed to the screen. Files can be browsed without knowing their exact name (by reading READMEs), but often users already know the pathname they want. The transfer reports completion status including bytes transferred and transfer speed (illustrating typical 1994 network performance).
sections.eli5: Here is what a real FTP session looks like: you connect, log in as anonymous, navigate folders, find a file (like an RFC), and download it. The server tells you what is happening at each step with status codes.

sections.title: Archive Site Etiquette
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that not all sites offering FTP permit anonymous transfers, and users should never attempt to use anonymous FTP where it has not been explicitly advertised. Archive site administrators maintain these services as a community contribution, rarely receiving full compensation for their time and effort. Users can make their jobs easier by following etiquette guidelines.

Key recommendations include checking with local support personnel before contacting archive administrators, restricting FTP access to non-prime hours (typically 19:00-06:00 local time at the site), being especially respectful for sites on other continents or across slow links, respecting limits on concurrent anonymous logins (waiting rather than retrying immediately if refused), and avoiding redundant storage by making files available to entire organizations rather than having each user download separately. If finding a useful program, users should notify their administrator for organization-wide installation, and inform others about interesting archive contents—but only maintain personal copies if willing to keep them current.
sections.eli5: Archive administrators are volunteers. Be polite: do not download during business hours, do not retry too fast if the site is full, and share good finds with your whole team instead of making everyone download separately.

references.text: Postel, J., and J. Reynolds, "File Transfer Protocol (FTP)", STD 9, RFC 959, USC/Information Sciences Institute, October 1985.
